correctness.rationale: The pre-existing exact fiber formula is independently reconstructed by parking preference choices. For any rising adjacent pair, the two altered suffix lengths and every possible later affected length are characterized precisely, yielding the exact product formula (1). Bounding its local factor and telescoping all possible later multipliers proves both sharp inequalities; explicit witnesses attain both bounds for all \(n\) and \(i\). A convex one-variable optimization proves the global maximum and its asymptotic. The standalone exact checker executes 475272 checks, including full permutations through \(n=8\) and independent direct parking preference enumeration through \(n=5\); no finite test is substituted for the general proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The strongest directly applicable results supply the measure’s probability mass function. Formula availability allows one to compute ratios for any given pair, but no identified stronger theorem gives, as a stated consequence with proved optimality, the extremal positionwise envelope \(1/(i+1)\) to \(i(n-i)/(i+1)\). The distinctive proof obligation is to maximize changes in all later suffix lengths simultaneously, achieved by explicit witnesses. There is a real residual risk that this bound was derived elsewhere from the classical identity.

originality.rationale: A sharp optimization over neighboring-permutation mass ratios and its non-monotonicity/linear-amplification consequences were not located in the inspected primary literature or result records. The exact parking-outcome mass law and global single-mass extrema are explicitly prior; the additional all-\(n\) edge optimization is not a mere renaming of them and requires tracking nonlocal affected suffix records. Residual possibility of previously published implicit or explicit coverage is acknowledged.

The 1999 Stanley book cited as precursor of the mass formula was not independently read; it is not asserted to contain no relevant optimization.

value.rationale: The result answers a natural structural question about a probabilistic measure on permutations beyond already known mass distributions: whether inserting one inversion always reduces probability and, if not, the sharp amplification at every location. It classifies all positions, establishes boundary-only monotonicity, identifies the first reversal at \(n=4\), and proves an optimal worst-case factor of linear order with extremizing positions at \(\sqrt n\) scale. These are nontrivial qualitative and quantitative properties of the outcome distribution, not a routine arbitrary numeric slice.
